title: Original-Vow Buddha-Recitation
author: Zhanran
excerpt: A: The original vow refers to the eighteenth of Amitābha Buddha's forty-eight great vows. (See further “The Original Vow of Amitābha Buddha.”) This eighteenth vow states: “If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings in the ten directions, with sincere mind and joyful faith, aspire to be born in my land, and who invoke even ten times, if they should not be reborn there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Excluded alone are those who commit the five grave offenses and those who slander the correct Dharma.”

inline.s: Q: What is original-vow Buddha-recitation?
A: The original vow refers to the eighteenth of the forty-eight great vows of Amitābha Buddha. (See further
The Original Vow of Amitābha Buddha
.) This eighteenth vow states:

“If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings in the ten directions who, with sincere mind and joyful faith, aspire to be born in my land, and who invoke [my name] even ten times, should not be reborn there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Excluded alone are those who commit the five grave offenses and those who slander the correct Dharma.”
(From the Sutra of Immeasurable Life spoken by the Buddha.) Regarding the meaning of the eighteenth vow, Master Daochuo has already explained it clearly in the Collection on Peace and Happiness:

“If there are sentient beings who, though they have done evil throughout their lives, at the moment of death keep up ten thoughts in succession and call upon my name, if they should not be reborn there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
Here Master Daochuo gives an exact explanation of the meaning of “even ten times” in the eighteenth vow:
At the moment of death, keep up ten thoughts in succession.
So original-vow Buddha-recitation is to recite the Buddha in reliance upon Amitābha Buddha's original vow (
that ten thoughts kept up in succession at the moment of death bring about rebirth directly
). Hence the essential point of original-vow Buddha-recitation is:
Ten thoughts in succession, repeated practice until it becomes innate.

To ensure that the ten thoughts in succession at the moment of death are accomplished, so as to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. On this, Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitābha Buddha, teaches:
It is precisely because calling the name is easy
(precisely because being mindful of the Buddha by invoking the name is easier than contemplating the Buddha)
, that a continued succession [of thoughts] brings rebirth
the thoughts of Buddha-recitation kept in succession at the moment of death bring rebirth
. If one can keep the thoughts in continuous succession and so continue until the end of life, then of ten, ten will be reborn, and of a hundred, a hundred will be reborn.
May all people reflect well upon this, and throughout walking, standing, sitting, and lying down must rouse their minds and restrain themselves
(rouse themselves and restrain themselves)
, and not neglect it by day or by night
(do not stop the succession of thoughts by day or by night)
. When the previous thought ends in death, the next thought brings rebirth. Forever enjoying the bliss of the unconditioned Dharma, and even attaining Buddhahood — how joyful this is!”
(For the commentary please see further
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching

[Continuity (xiangxu)] The thoughts of Buddha-recitation are linked together without being interrupted by wandering thoughts. [Practice until it becomes innate (jixi chengxing)] Through repeated practice, make it into an instinct.
However,

the Original Vow school has twisted the “even ten times” of the eighteenth vow into meaning reciting the Buddha ten times with a scattered mind in everyday life. Therefore they proclaim “calling the name guarantees rebirth” (as long as one recites the Buddha a little in ordinary life, one is certain to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss at death), and so there is no need to practice, no need to uphold the precepts, no need to do good, no need to purify one's own mind — even committing evil all one's life is of no consequence, because “the evil person is the true object [of deliverance] of Amitābha Buddha's salvation”; this is Amitābha Buddha's original vow. For example, Master Huijing says in The Essential Meaning of Master Shandao: “He does not realize that the purpose of the Contemplation Sutra is to reveal the original vow of Amitābha: the evil person as the true object.” Master Hōnen says: “If a person commits the five grave offenses

(the five grave offenses: five kinds of crimes utterly opposed to principle — killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, drawing blood from the body of a Buddha, and causing division in the Sangha. These five are utterly evil deeds; committing any one of them plunges one into the Interminable Hell, and so they are also called the “karma of the interminable”)
, and hears the six-syllable name
(hears “Namo Amitābha Buddha”)
, the fiery chariot departs of itself
(the fiery chariot of hell departs of itself)

, and the lotus throne comes to welcome him.” (Quoted from the Forty-Eight Dharma Words of Master Hōnen compiled by Master Huijing, also titled The Dharma Words of Peace of Mind for Buddha-Recitation.) This means that a great evil person who has committed the five grave offenses, so long as he hears the Buddha's name, is thereupon reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss to enjoy all bliss forever.
This is what the Original Vow school calls “original-vow Buddha-recitation”!
calling the name guarantees rebirth”
and
“the evil person is the true object”
these two are the
essential point
of what the Original Vow school calls “original-vow Buddha-recitation”. Master Hōnen says: “The
essential point
of the Pure Land school lies in this — whoever it may be, if one recites the Buddha, all are reborn. Even a person of evil without parallel
(without equal)
in the world, if he invokes Namo Amitābha Buddha, even with a single thought he attains rebirth as well.” (See further
Master Hōnen's “Dharma Words of Peace of Mind for Buddha-Recitation”

.) They cleverly exploit human weaknesses — fear of difficulty, the desire to take the easy way, attachment to worldly pleasures — to win over believers. “Calling the name guarantees rebirth” is the theoretical basis for monastics not needing to practice, and “the evil person is the true object” is the theoretical basis for monastics not needing to uphold the precepts or to abandon evil and cultivate good. Thus the monastic has degenerated from a cultivator into a professional monk who neither upholds the precepts nor practices, and who may do anything at all — keep his hair, eat meat, take a wife, commit evil
This is utterly inverted teaching! For the refutation of these fallacies, please see further
The Original Vow School Is a Non-Buddhist Cult Attached to Buddhism

Q: An article says: “The great master Huiyuan of Jingying Temple in the Sui dynasty and others held that the power of scattered good deeds is slight and cannot eradicate the grave offense of the five, and so one cannot be reborn. Master Shandao of the Tang dynasty, however, held that with original-vow Buddha-recitation, even if one merely calls the Buddha's name with a scattered mind, because one relies upon the power of Amitābha Buddha's vow, one can still attain rebirth.” Did Master Shandao really say this?
A:
This is a slander of Master Shandao!
Master Shandao always advocated single-minded Buddha-recitation
, and he never said anything like “
with original-vow Buddha-recitation, even if one merely calls the Buddha's name with a scattered mind, because one relies upon the power of Amitābha Buddha's vow, one can still attain rebirth
” and so forth. All this is the Original Vow school taking Master Shandao's teachings out of context, willfully distorting them, or fabricating them out of nothing. Simply compare their lies with
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching
and the true and the false will be seen at once. Below I will cite only three of Master Shandao's teachings on how to recite the Buddha, and that will be enough to expose their lies.
1. In the Four-Volume Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra, Master Shandao teaches:
Single-minded
and exclusive mindfulness of the name of Amitābha Buddha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of whether the time is long or short,
never letting go in thought after thought
— this is called the karma of right samādhi,
because it accords with that Buddha's vow

Translation: Single-mindedly and exclusively invoking the name of Amitābha Buddha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of how long or short the time, and never letting go in thought after thought — this is called the karma of right samādhi, because it accords with the vow of Amitābha Buddha.

[Single-mindedness (yixin)] Master Tanluan teaches in the Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth: Single-mindedness means thought after thought in continuous succession, with no other thoughts interspersed. (See further
Master Tanluan's Pure Land Teaching

.) [Never letting go (niannian bushe)] Every thought is the name of Amitābha Buddha. [Right samādhi (zhengding)] Correct meditation. When body and mind are pure and clear, without scatteredness, this is called “right samādhi”. [Karma (ye)] The activities of body, speech, and mind.
Here Master Shandao teaches:

“Single-mindedly and exclusively invoking the name of Amitābha Buddha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of whether the time is long or short, never letting go in thought after thought”
— this is
“because it accords with that Buddha's vow”
(because it accords with the vow of Amitābha Buddha.)
From this we know that for sentient beings to
invoke the Buddha single-mindedly, never letting go in thought after thought
, is to accord with the vow of Amitābha Buddha. Then
reciting the Buddha with a scattered mind is contrary to the vow of Amitābha Buddha!
2. In the Four-Volume Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra,
Master Shandao further teaches:

“Now there are two kinds of practice: the first is proper practice; the second is mixed practice. What is called proper practice is to practice in reliance upon the sutras of rebirth — this is called proper practice. What are they?
Single-mindedly
recite this Contemplation Sutra, the Amitābha Sutra, the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, and so forth,
single-mindedly
focus thought, contemplate, and be mindful of the sublimities of the two kinds of reward of that land. If one prostrates, then
single-mindedly
prostrate only to that Buddha; if one invokes with the mouth, then
single-mindedly
invoke only that Buddha; if one praises and makes offerings, then
single-mindedly
praise and make offerings only [to him].
This is called proper practice
(From the Four-Volume Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra.)
This means that single-minded Buddha-recitation is the proper practice. Then, Buddha-recitation with a scattered mind is not the proper practice.
[The sutras of rebirth (wangsheng jing)] These are the three Pure Land sutras: the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, the Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life, and the Amitābha Sutra.

[The sublimities of the two rewards (erbao zhuangyan)] The sublimities of the two rewards, the dependent and the proper. [Dependent and proper (yizheng)] The dependent reward and the proper reward. The dependent reward is the retribution in which one dwells, such as the land, the earth, houses, and implements — that is, the environment of life. The proper reward is the body and mind of the Buddha and of sentient beings; this is the very substance of the retribution received in response to past karmic causes. The proper rewards of the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss are two: first, the sublimity of the sovereign, namely Amitābha Buddha (the Buddha of Immeasurable Life); second, the sublimity of the holy assembly, namely the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and devas of the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. (See further the Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life.)
3. In [the teaching] on the Proper and Mixed Two Kinds of Practice of Pure Karma, he teaches:
“It is precisely because calling the name is easy
(precisely because being mindful of the Buddha by invoking the name is easier than contemplating the Buddha)
, that a continued succession [of thoughts] brings rebirth
(the ten thoughts kept up in succession at the moment of death bring rebirth)
. If one can keep the thoughts in continuous succession and so continue until the end of life, then of ten, ten will be reborn, and of a hundred, a hundred will be reborn.
May all people reflect well upon this, and throughout walking, standing, sitting, and lying down must rouse their minds and restrain themselves
(rouse themselves and restrain themselves)
, and not neglect it by day or by night
(do not stop the succession of thoughts by day or by night)
. When the previous thought ends in death, the next thought brings rebirth. Forever enjoying the bliss of the unconditioned Dharma, and even attaining Buddhahood — how joyful this is!”
(For the commentary please see further
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching
[Thought after thought in succession (niannian xiangxu)] The thoughts of Buddha-recitation are linked together without being interrupted by wandering thoughts.
Here Master Shandao states it clearly:
“If one can keep the thoughts in continuous succession and so continue until the end of life, then of ten, ten will be reborn, and of a hundred, a hundred will be reborn.”
And
May all people
reflect well upon this, and throughout walking, standing, sitting, and lying down must rouse their minds and restrain themselves, not neglecting it by day or by night.”
Where does he ever speak of “
with original-vow Buddha-recitation, even if one merely calls the Buddha's name with a scattered mind, because one relies upon the power of Amitābha Buddha's vow, one can still attain rebirth
